title: Want to Give Back This Diwali? How to Find and Vet a Cause That Matters
excerpt: Pick the cause first, then check the organisation on a vetted platform and on GuideStar India — and keep the acknowledgement, receipt and Form 10BE that make a donation traceable.
body:
• Start from the cause, then vet the organisation: use a platform that lists vetted nonprofits and check its due-diligence and update record before donating.
  • Give, at give.do, says donors can search more than 3,000 vetted NGOs by cause or organisation name and receive an official email acknowledgement for each donation.
  • GuideStar India lets you search nonprofits by certification level, geography, cause and financials, including tax benefits and FCRA eligibility.
  • For Indian tax relief, Give says donations can be claimed under Section 80G, with Form 10BE issued by the receiving organisation by the end of May of the next financial year.

Diwali giving is easy to start and easy to get wrong. A forwarded appeal can name a real problem and still leave a donor with no way to tell who will receive the money, what it will fund, or whether any record will follow. The practical fix is to slow the decision down by one step: pick the cause first, then choose an organisation through a platform that publishes how it checks the nonprofits it lists.

Start with the cause, not the appeal

On Give, donors browse causes that include children, elderly care, animal welfare, health, poverty alleviation, disability, women, disaster relief, environment, art and culture, sports and human rights, or search directly for a specific NGO they already know. Give says its community of more than 1 million individual donors supports nonprofits across India, and that a donor can read how an NGO is addressing an issue before deciding. That order matters. A cause you can name — girls returning to school, meals for malnourished children and elders, care for abandoned elders — gives you a testable claim to check after you give, rather than a general feeling to trust.

How to vet before you pay

Give says it regularly conducts periodic due diligence of NGOs to ensure organisations meet its standards on compliance, transparency and impact, and that donors can check an NGO's fundraiser page for periodic updates on how funds are being used. After a donation, the platform sends an official email acknowledgement. Those three things — a stated due-diligence process, published updates, and a receipt trail — are the minimum to look for on any platform, not just this one.

GuideStar India offers a second, independent check. It describes itself as a repository of nonprofit profiles that can be searched by certification level, geography — down to state, district and pincode — cause, and financials, including size, tax benefits and FCRA eligibility. Its certification rests on a seven-pillar assessment covering situation analysis, theory of change, programme intervention, infrastructure, finance and compliance, governance and accountability, and evidence of impact. If an organisation appears on a donation platform but has no findable profile, financial information or certification record, that gap is itself information.

Tax and records, as the platform states them

Give states that a donation to an NGO on its platform can be claimed for tax exemption under Section 80G of the Income Tax Act, allowing a portion or the entire donated amount to be deducted from taxable income. It says the donation receipt is sent within two weeks, and that Form 10BE, which validates the deduction and is issued by the organisation receiving the donation, arrives by the end of May of the next financial year for use when filing returns. Keep both documents with the acknowledgement email. Tax treatment depends on the donor's own situation, and neither platform summary here replaces the receiving organisation's documentation.

A steadier option: monthly giving

Give promotes monthly missions starting at ₹600 a month, arguing that a steady contribution lets an NGO plan — a student supported through a school year, or long-term medical treatment in a remote area — rather than plan around a single festival spike. Its named missions include Every Girl in School, No Child Orphaned, Protect Abandoned Elders, Feed the Hungry, End Period Poverty and Clean India's Environment. A monthly commitment is also a vetting device: you can read the updates from a small recurring gift before deciding whether the organisation has earned a larger one.

The Diwali test, then, is simple. Name the cause, find the organisation on a vetted platform, cross-check it on GuideStar India, keep the acknowledgement, receipt and Form 10BE, and follow the updates after the festival lights come down.
